To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) we can learn radiance functions of clouds from a few examples, (b) we can learn the radiance function of clouds using a neural network with residual connections and a hierarchical descriptor, (c) we can use a block network design that progressively feeds the hierarchical descriptor into each block and, (d) the block design can be used with any neural network architecture.

we propose a new method for rendering of clouds based on radiance-predictive deep learning and hierarchical descriptors, and demonstrate that it can be applied to high-quality rendering of clouds in real-time.

(1) we present a novel method that efficiently renders images of atmospheric clouds, (2) we use neural networks to pre-learn the distribution of radiant flux, (3) the neural networks are trained using Monte Carlo integration of the radiance transport equation, (4) we use the trained neural network during rendering to predict the radiance function, and (5) we show that the proposed approach produces images of atmospheric clouds with a quality that is nearly indistinguishable to reference solutions within seconds

The main takeaway from our work is that

neural networks can be used for predicting the radiance function in complex media, such as clouds, and, more generally, for rendering scenes that are difficult or impossible to render with Monte Carlo or diffusion-based methods alone.
, for a class of problems, deep neural networks can be used to predict the radiance function from a set of descriptors that encode the spatial and directional properties of the scene.

, by prelearning the radiance function from a large number of exemplars, it is possible to efficiently render complex phenomena with high albedo that are difficult to capture using Monte Carlo integration alone.
